instances.brief: {{node_name}} is returning 5xx to every upstream caller. The app log covers the last 10 minutes. Find the line that explains why the process stopped accepting requests.
instances.teaches: The earliest error in a causal chain is the root cause. Errors that arrive after a process crashes are blast-radius: they tell you what broke downstream, not what broke first.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Selecting an 'upstream timed out' or 'connection reset' ERROR line misidentifies blast-radius as cause: those errors are what other services see after the process dies — not what killed it. Error rate stays at 100% and reputation falls 4 points.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The upstream errors and connection resets begin at 14:02:11 — the same second as the FATAL. They are downstream consequences of the process exiting, not the trigger. The trigger is the FATAL heap exhaustion line.

instances.reveal: GC pause duration rose steadily from 180ms to 1900ms over two minutes as the heap approached its 512 MB limit. At 14:02:11 the V8 runtime could not allocate further and the process terminated with 'heap out of memory'. Every ERROR line after that timestamp is an upstream caller seeing a dead socket — they are the blast radius, not the cause. Restarting the process clears the heap and restores service; the GC escalation tells you to investigate the memory leak separately.

instances.brief: Error rate on {{node_name}} jumped after a recent deploy. The log spans the last 30 minutes. Identify the line that first reveals what the deploy broke.
instances.teaches: Correlate the first new error signature with the change boundary. A pre-existing ERROR that predates the deploy is unrelated noise; the first error whose timestamp follows the deploy boundary is the regression.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Selecting the disk-usage ERROR at 13:40 identifies noise that predates the deploy by 22 minutes — it cannot be the regression. Selecting a timeout ERROR at 14:02:10+ misses the actual first failure signature; error rate stays at 9% and rollback is not applied.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The disk-usage ERROR at 13:40 is pre-existing noise with no relation to the deploy. The timeout ERRORs that begin at 14:02:10 are a secondary cascade — the TypeError was already firing for 3 seconds before the first timeout appeared. The first line that carries a new error signature introduced by v2.14.0 is line 15.

instances.reveal: The deploy boundary is the INFO line at 14:02:00. The first ERROR after that boundary is a TypeError at 14:02:07 — a null-dereference inside PriceFormatter.format that v2.14.0 introduced when it restructured the price object shape. The disk-usage ERROR at 13:40 is pre-existing and unrelated; the timeout ERRORs at 14:02:10 are a secondary cascade caused by the TypeError failing requests. Rolling back to v2.13.1 removes the null-dereference and stops both the TypeError and the timeout cascade.

instances.brief: The Postgres slow-query log on {{node_name}} shows elevated p95 latency since 12:00. Two query patterns are flagged. Find the line that points to the query that is actually hurting production traffic.
instances.teaches: Total cost is duration × frequency. A single 12-second query that runs once per night costs the database 12 seconds of wall time. A 420 ms query running 20 times per minute costs 8400 ms per minute — 700× more throughput drain. Index the high-frequency path.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Selecting the analytics_rollup query at 12:00:57 (12,400 ms) focuses on duration alone. That query runs once — 12,400 ms of total cost. The orders query runs ~20 times per minute at 420 ms each, costing ~8,400 ms per minute continuously. P95 stays elevated and the index is applied to the wrong table.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The analytics_rollup query is a scheduled nightly report. Its 12-second runtime happens once and is expected. The SELECT on orders runs continuously — every 3 seconds across all customer lookups — doing a full sequential scan of 4.2 M rows on each call. Frequency × duration is what fills the connection pool and drives p95 up.

instances.reveal: The orders query (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1) appears 42 times in this 75-second window — roughly 20 times per minute. Each execution scans all 4.2 M rows because there is no index on customer_id. At 420 ms each, that is 8,400 ms per minute of sequential scan load, filling the connection pool and raising p95. The analytics_rollup query at 12,400 ms looks dramatic but runs once (a scheduled nightly report, marked as such in its log line). An index on orders(customer_id) drops the orders query to under 5 ms.
